841.title: Mystery plays
841.hook: townspeople acted the Bible on wagons: the shipwrights built Noah's ark
841.howItsDone: Some English towns, including York and Chester, still stage their mystery plays, sometimes on wagons in the streets, and some churches put on nativity plays with children at Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nubia's churches, faces found under the sand by the Nile. Your line was remembered churches. Whose name did you say aloud? Day eight hundred forty-one.

A summer morning in an English town, and a wooden wagon creaks around the corner, pulled into the street. On it, a man with a hammer is building a boat. He's playing Noah. The men helping him on stage build real boats all week, because they're the town's shipwrights. The wagon moves on to the next corner, and another wagon rolls up behind it with the next story. On one of them, later, the crowd laughs when Noah's wife refuses to get on board. All day long, the whole Bible comes down the street. Today: mystery plays.

Mystery plays were cycles of short Bible plays, put on by ordinary townspeople in English towns like York and Chester. They usually ran from creation to the last judgment: the fall, Noah, Abraham and Isaac, the shepherds at Bethlehem, the crucifixion, the empty tomb. Each play was given to a trade guild, and the guilds often got the scene that fit their work. In York, the shipwrights staged the building of the ark. In Genesis, God tells Noah, in the King James Bible, "Make thee an ark of gopher wood." And then, "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." Who better to swing those hammers than the people who built boats for a living? Each play went up on a pageant wagon, a stage on wheels, and the wagons moved through the town, stopping at set places so different crowds could see each scene in turn. The plays were in English, the language people spoke at home, at a time when church services were in Latin. They mixed holy and ordinary. Shepherds grumble about the cold before the angel comes. Noah's wife, in some plays, would rather stay with her friends than climb into the ark. People laughed, and then they watched a carpenter's son die on a cross. A town that acted these stories year after year carried them in its body: the lines, the hammers, the costumes kept in a guild's chest. Scripture wasn't only something read to them. It was something they did.

Here's the practice: act out a story with a child, or plan to. Pick one Bible story you know well: Noah and the ark, the lost sheep, the Good Samaritan. Cast it in your head. Who would play the boat-builder? Who gets to be the stubborn one? What would you use for props, a broom, a blanket, a cardboard box? If there's a child in your life, plan to act it with them this week. If not, walk through the scene yourself, just to see it from the inside. If you pray, you can give thanks for the story. The bell holds the time.
Mystery plays. Cycles of Bible plays acted by townspeople and their guilds, on wagons, in English, from creation to the last judgment.
Your line: the bible on wagons. Today, tell one story aloud instead of explaining it: with a voice for each character, even if your only audience is the dog. Day eight hundred forty-one.

842.title: Pilgrims' roads
842.hook: Canterbury, Santiago, Rome: people walked a long way to reach a holy place
842.howItsDone: Christians, and others too, still walk the Camino to Santiago de Compostela, carrying a scallop shell and collecting stamps in a pilgrim passport, and pilgrims still travel to Rome, Canterbury, the Holy Land and other shrines.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mystery plays, the Bible acted on wagons by townspeople, with shipwrights building the ark. Your line was the bible on wagons. Which story did you tell aloud? Day eight hundred forty-two.

Why would anyone leave home, on foot, to reach a grave? Part of the answer hangs from a walking stick: a scallop shell, tied on with a bit of cord. That's how you'd know someone was on the road to Santiago. Blisters on their feet. A small bag. A hat against the sun. They left home long ago, and they won't sleep in their own bed for a long time yet. In Chaucer's tales, a company on horseback trades stories on the way to Canterbury. On another road, travelers climb toward Rome. Different roads, one question underneath. Today: pilgrims' roads.

Each road ended at a grave or a shrine. Rome, where tradition says Peter and Paul are buried. Santiago de Compostela, in Spain, where tradition places the tomb of James the apostle, and where the scallop shell became the pilgrim's badge. Canterbury, in England, where Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in his own cathedral and then honored as a saint. People went for many reasons. To ask for healing. To give thanks. To do penance for a wrong. To keep a promise. Some, honestly, for the adventure, and Chaucer's Canterbury Tales is full of pilgrims who talk more than they pray. But the road itself mattered. Leaving home meant leaving your comfort, your title, your routine. On the road, a merchant and a farmer could sleep in the same hostel and eat the same soup. Monasteries and towns along the way took pilgrims in. The Bible gave them words for this. Hebrews says the faithful of old confessed, in the King James Bible, "that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." And a Psalm that longs for God's house blesses the one "in whose heart are the ways of them." Tradition says pilgrims sang another Psalm as they climbed toward Jerusalem: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Christians have not all agreed about pilgrimage. Some reformers later criticized it, saying God is just as near at home. Catholic and Orthodox Christians still go, and so do others, on foot. And some walkers say the same surprising thing: the road became the prayer.
screen: `A GRAVE OR A SHRINE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere on purpose. Not in these two minutes: choose it now. Think of a place within walking distance that means something to you: a church, a park, a grave, a tree, a friend's front door. Picture the route. Picture setting out, without your phone in your hand, with one intention to carry: thanks, a worry, a person. If you pray, you can pray as you walk. If you don't, let each step be the attention. The bell holds the time.
Pilgrims' roads. The roads to holy places like Rome, Santiago and Canterbury, walked for healing, thanks or penance, where the journey itself becomes part of the prayer.
Your line: the road is the prayer. Today, take the walk you chose, even a short one, and go slowly enough to notice the way. Day eight hundred forty-two.

843.title: Beads of prayer
843.hook: counting prayers on beads grew in the middle ages; the Orthodox use knotted prayer ropes
843.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary on a string of beads, alone or together, and Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer on a knotted prayer rope; some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pilgrims' roads to Rome, Santiago and Canterbury. Your line was the road is the prayer. Where did your walk take you? Day eight hundred forty-three.

A grandmother's hands, folded in her lap, with a loop of beads running through her fingers. Her lips move. Every few seconds, her thumb slides one bead along. In another house, in another church, a monk holds a loop of black wool, tied in thick knots, and his thumb moves the same way. Bead, word. Knot, word. Neither of them is looking at their hands. The hands are keeping count so the heart doesn't have to. Today: beads of prayer.
screen: `A LOOP OF BEADS IN HER FINGERS.`

segments.voice: Christians counting prayers is an old habit. Tradition remembers desert monks who counted their prayers with pebbles, moving one stone from one pile to another. Later, in the West, people threaded beads on a string to count the Lord's Prayer, the Our Father, again and again. In the middle ages these strings grew into the rosary, where Catholics pray the Hail Mary in sets, each set beginning with the Our Father, while they think about scenes from the lives of Jesus and Mary. In the East, Orthodox monks use a prayer rope, a loop of wool knotted again and again, and with each knot they say the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Orthodox monks tell a story about it. A holy monk tied knots in a cord to count his prayers, and the devil kept untying them. So the monk learned to tie each knot as a little web of crosses, and the devil couldn't undo them. Whatever its origin, the story says something true about how these ropes are meant: each knot is made to hold. Why repeat a prayer at all? Paul tells one church, in the King James Bible, "Pray without ceasing." Repetition is one way people have tried to obey that line. But Jesus also says, in Matthew, "use not vain repetitions." Some Protestants are cautious about counted prayers for that reason, and pray in their own words. Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that a prayer said from the heart isn't vain, however often it's said. Each side reads the same Gospel seriously.
screen: `BEADS FOR THE OUR FATHER, THEN THE ROSARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten prayers on your fingers. Rest your hands in your lap. Choose one short line. If you pray, it might be the Jesus Prayer, or the first line of the Our Father, or a line from a Psalm. If you don't, it might be a single word like thanks, or the name of someone you love. Touch your thumb to one fingertip and say the line, slowly. Then the next fingertip. Ten times, across both hands. If you lose count, start again without fuss. The bell holds the time.
Jesus Prayer. The words Orthodox monks repeat on a knotted prayer rope, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, so the hands keep count and the heart can pray.
Your line: counting love. Today, count ten good things about someone who's hard to love, one finger at a time, before you speak to them. Day eight hundred forty-three.

knotted wool for the Jesus Prayer

844.title: The poor people's Bible
844.hook: colored windows told Bible stories to people who couldn't read
844.howItsDone: Stained glass windows still tell Bible stories in churches of different traditions, and churches sometimes hold tours or talks that walk people through a window's story from bottom to top.

segments.voice: Yesterday, beads of prayer, the rosary and the Jesus Prayer on the knotted rope. Your line was counting love. Whose ten good things did you count? Day eight hundred forty-four.

Late afternoon, and a patch of blue and red light is sliding slowly across a stone floor. Follow it up to where it comes from, and there's a window, high in the wall, made of small pieces of colored glass. Look closer, and the colors become people. A man in a boat. A woman at a well. A shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. A whole story, told in light, pane by pane, from the bottom of the window to the top. Today: the poor people's Bible.

Stained glass. The glass gets its color as it's made, and then the details, faces, hands, the folds of a robe, are painted on with dark paint and fired so they hold. Lead strips join the pieces like the lines in a coloring book. In the great churches of the middle ages, windows like these told the Bible's stories, and the lives of the saints, to people who couldn't read. A pope, Gregory the Great, wrote to a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his church. Don't destroy them, Gregory told him. What writing gives to those who can read, a picture gives to those who can't. Some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible. Some historians wonder how much anyone could make out of a window that high. But even from the floor, the light did its work. Windows often paired stories: one from the Old Testament beside one from the New, so that, say, Jonah coming out of the fish sits near Jesus rising from the tomb. Often you read them from the bottom up. There's a line that fits. In the King James Bible, John writes, "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not." A stained glass window is dark from the outside. You only see its story from inside, when the sun comes through. Christians have not all loved these windows. In some times and places, reformers broke them, believing images drew worship away from God. Other Protestants kept and made new ones. Churches of different traditions use them still.
screen: `COLOR IN THE GLASS, FACES PAINTED ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at light through colored glass. If you can, find some: a bottle, a glass of juice or wine, a colored jar, a window, even a phone screen turned to a single color. Hold it up to a lamp or the window. Watch the color the light makes. Notice that the glass does nothing on its own; it waits for the light. If you pray, you can give thanks for the light. If you don't, simply watch it. The bell holds the time.
Stained glass. Colored glass, painted and leaded into windows that tell the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.
Your line: light tells stories. Today, notice where the light falls in a room you love, and what it shows you that you'd missed. Day eight hundred forty-four.

845.title: Monasteries as hospitals
845.hook: monks kept books, schools, herb gardens and infirmaries
845.howItsDone: Christian religious orders and churches still run hospitals, clinics and hospices around the world, and some monasteries still keep herb gardens and infirmaries for their own sick members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stained glass, the poor people's Bible, told in light. Your line was light tells stories. Where did the light fall in your room? Day eight hundred forty-five.

Sage. Rue. Fennel. Mint. Small square beds of herbs, laid out in neat rows behind a stone wall. A monk in a dark habit kneels between them, cutting leaves into a basket. He isn't cooking dinner. He's carrying the basket a few steps across the yard, to a long room where sick men lie in beds, and he's going to make a warm drink for a feverish old brother and a poultice for a farmer's cut hand. Today: monasteries as hospitals.

In the middle ages, a monastery might be the place where the sick were cared for. The reason goes back to a rule. Benedict's Rule for monks gives a whole chapter to the sick, and says care for them comes before everything else, because in serving them, the monks serve Christ. Behind that is Jesus's scene in Matthew where visiting the sick is visiting him, the same scene that kept some at the bedside in the plague years. The letter of James asks, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him". So monasteries set aside an infirmary, a room for the sick, with a brother in charge of it. They kept a garden of healing herbs near it. An old plan for an ideal monastery, kept at the abbey of Saint Gall, puts a physician's herb garden right beside the infirmary. And the monks kept books, a slower kind of care. In the scriptorium, monks and nuns copied scripture, prayers, and old books of medicine and learning, page by page. Some monasteries ran schools, where boys, and in convents girls, learned to read. None of this was the main point. The main point, for the monks, was prayer, the hours of psalms sung through the day and night. But prayer that takes Matthew seriously spills out into rooms with beds, gardens with herbs, and shelves with books. You could call these communities keepers of the light: the lamp kept burning in the chapel, and the lamp kept burning by a sick bed, and the lamp kept burning over a page.
screen: `BOOKS, SCHOOLS, AND A LAMP BY THE BED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grow or buy one herb. Choose it now. Picture a small pot on a windowsill. Basil, mint, rosemary, thyme, whatever you like. Picture watering it, pinching off a leaf, smelling your fingers. Now think of someone who's sick or worn out, someone you could bring something to: a cup of mint tea, soup with a few leaves on top, or just your company. If you pray, you can pray for them. If you don't, hold them in mind, with the smell of the herb. The bell holds the time.
Infirmary. The room for the sick that medieval monasteries kept, with a garden of healing herbs close by, following Benedict's Rule to care for the sick before everything else.
Your line: keepers of the light. Today, get the herb, and use it for someone else: tea, soup, or a sprig on a plate for a person who's tired. Day eight hundred forty-five.

846.title: Guests as Christ
846.hook: the Rule of Benedict: let all guests be received as Christ (Rule 53)
846.howItsDone: Benedictine monasteries and convents keep guest houses where visitors can stay, pray with the community and share meals, and the porter or guest master greets them in the spirit of Rule 53.

segments.voice: Yesterday, monasteries as hospitals: herbs by the infirmary, books in the scriptorium. Your line was keepers of the light. Who got your herb? Day eight hundred forty-six.

A knock at the monastery gate, after dark. Rain. On the other side of the door, a stranger: muddy boots, a wet cloak, nobody the porter has ever seen. Could be a pilgrim. Could be a thief. Could be a lord in disguise or a beggar with nowhere else to go. The old porter gets up from his bench by the gate, and the words he's been taught to say come out first, before any question about who this is: thanks be to God. Today: guests as Christ.

The Rule of Benedict, the guidebook for monks we met yesterday, has a chapter on guests, and it opens with a startling instruction. Let every guest who comes be received as Christ. Why? Because, the Rule says, Christ himself will one day say the words of Matthew's Gospel, in the King James Bible: "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." So the stranger at the gate is not an interruption. In the Rule's eyes, the stranger is Christ, arriving in disguise. And the chapter gets specific. The superior and the brothers go out to meet the guest. They pray together, and then exchange the kiss of peace. The abbot pours water over the guest's hands, and he and the community wash the guest's feet. Visitors are fed. And the Rule adds a line that is easy to miss: the poor and pilgrims are to be shown the most care, because in them Christ is received more especially. The rich, it notes dryly, get respect anyway, because people are wary of them. Then it is practical too. The abbot and the guests have their own kitchen, so people arriving at all hours don't disturb the brothers. Holiness with a spare kitchen. The first letter of Peter puts the same welcome in a few plain words: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Without grudging, even at the door after dark. The idea underneath doesn't need a monastery. Every door, sooner or later, has a stranger on the other side.
screen: `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YE TOOK ME IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone the way the Rule welcomes a guest. Think of the people who will come to your door today, in person, on a screen, in your inbox. A coworker who always needs something. A delivery driver. A child who interrupts. Someone you'd rather avoid. Choose one. Picture them arriving, and picture yourself standing up, going to meet them, glad they came. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind kindly. The bell holds the time.
Hospes. The Latin word for guest, and also host, in the Rule of Benedict's chapter that says every guest should be received as Christ.
Your line: receive them as christ. Today, when the person you chose turns up, stand up, look up, or put the phone down, and greet them first. Day eight hundred forty-six.

847.title: Margery Kempe
847.hook: a loud, weeping English pilgrim who dictated her life to a scribe, and wouldn't stop crying in church
847.howItsDone: Christians today read The Book of Margery Kempe as a window into late medieval devotion, and some find in it permission for loud, emotional prayer; the Church of England remembers her in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rule of Benedict and the knock at the monastery door: hospes, guests as Christ. Your line was receive them as christ. Who came to your door, and how did you open it? Day eight hundred forty-seven.

A sermon is under way in an English church, and a woman in white is sobbing. Not quietly. Loudly enough that the preacher stops. Some of the congregation glare. Some mutter that she's faking, or sick, or showing off. One friar, her own book says, refuses to preach while she's in the building. She is a married woman from the town of Lynn, a mother, a former businesswoman who once ran a brewery that failed. She can't read or write. And she has decided to tell her whole life anyway, out loud, to a scribe who will write it down. Today: Margery Kempe.
screen: `SHE TELLS HER LIFE TO A SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: The Book of Margery Kempe is her story in her own telling, though she never calls herself I. She calls herself this creature. This creature went to Jerusalem. This creature was rebuked. It is not a polished book. It's restless, funny in places, and honest about how much she annoyed people. The tears are the center of it. On pilgrimage in Jerusalem, the Book says, standing where Jesus was crucified, she fell down and cried out as if her heart would burst, and after that the crying came back again and again for years. It came when she thought of the Passion, when she saw a baby boy, when she saw a man being beaten. Fellow pilgrims got so tired of her that they left her behind. Clergy questioned her. More than once she was accused of heresy, and more than once she talked her way out of it. So was it holiness, or something else? Her neighbors argued about that, and readers still do. The Book doesn't settle it. But it does record a visit she made to Julian, the anchoress at Norwich. Margery poured out her fears, and Julian, the Book says, told her that the Holy Spirit never moves a soul against love, and that a soul's tears can be a sign of the Spirit at work. Then, the Book adds, the two women talked together for days. The Gospels show Jesus weeping too. The King James Bible gives it in two words: "Jesus wept." Margery's neighbors found her tears too much. She kept weeping, and kept going.
screen: `CRYING AT THE PLACE OF THE CROSS.`
`JULIAN SAYS: TEARS CAN BE A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself be a bit too much. Not loud in a church, just a little more than usual. Settle, and breathe. Notice what's there right now, without trimming it down. If it's sadness, let it be the size it is. If it's gladness, the same. If nothing much is there, that's fine too. For the rest of the day, think of one thing you usually hold back: a laugh, a thank-you said with feeling, a song in the car. If you pray, you can bring whatever is there to God as it is, not tidied first. The bell holds the time.
Margery Kempe. An English wife, mother and pilgrim who wept loudly at prayer, told her life to a scribe, and called herself this creature.
Your line: tears are allowed. Today, if something moves you, a song, a story, a stranger's kindness, let it show a little, instead of swallowing it. Day eight hundred forty-seven.

fork.setup: you're Margery, in church. the sermon touches you and the tears start coming, loud. people are turning around. what do you do?
options: slip out quietly before anyone notices.
try to swallow it, and fail.
decide never to go to church again.
fork.reveal: the Book says she tried to hold the crying back, and it came anyway. she kept going to church, and on pilgrimage, tears and all.

trapdoor: what you thought: a medieval woman who cried a lot.
what it means: a wife, mother and pilgrim who wept at prayer, was rebuked for it, and told her own life to a scribe.
what a scholar hears: a book where the writer calls herself this creature, records her talk with Julian of Norwich, and leaves open whether her tears were holy.

sources.ref: The Book of Margery Kempe (Book I: the scribe; 'this creature'; the brewery; Jerusalem and Calvary; the visit to Julian; fellow pilgrims; accusations of heresy)
